name: THE BROTHER CAN YOU ASPARAGUS A DIME? BURGER

recipe.history:
Asparagus is one of the most ancient cultivated vegetables in the world, with records of its use stretching back more than two thousand years to ancient Egypt, Greece, and Rome. The Romans were particularly devoted to asparagus — Emperor Augustus is said to have coined the phrase 'velocius quam asparagi coquantur' (faster than you can cook asparagus) as a metaphor for speed, and Roman legions carried asparagus seeds across Europe as they expanded their territory. The plant is native to the eastern Mediterranean and western Asia, thriving in coastal and semi-arid soils, and its cultivation spread westward through Roman influence and eastward via trade routes. White asparagus, produced by mounding earth over the emerging spears to prevent photosynthesis and chlorophyll development, became a delicacy of northern European courts — particularly German and Dutch — where it is still celebrated as the 'white gold' of spring. Green asparagus dominated in southern Europe and eventually in America, where the rich alluvial soils of California and New Jersey became the primary growing regions.

Asparagus found its way into American burger culture through the farm-to-table movement of the 1990s and 2000s, when chefs began treating seasonal vegetables as featured ingredients rather than garnishes. The bold, slightly bitter, and distinctly mineral flavor of fresh asparagus grilled over high heat — with its tips charring and its stalks becoming tender — creates a textural and flavor bridge between the vegetable world and the beef world. Asparagus pesto, made by blanching and processing the stalks with Parmigiano, garlic, lemon, and good olive oil, uses the vegetable in a completely different register: smooth, bright, and herbaceous, it functions as both condiment and sauce. The combination of grilled whole spears and the pesto doubles the asparagus presence without redundancy.

Asparagus is the vegetable I most associate with the specific feeling of spring arriving after a long winter. The first asparagus at the farmers' market — thin, tightly furled, snapping cleanly when bent — is a reliable signal that the season has turned. I once ate an entire pound of asparagus for lunch, roasted simply with olive oil and salt, standing at my kitchen counter the first week they appeared at the market, because I had been waiting for them since November. The pesto came from a need to use up the tough ends I had cut off before roasting — blended with Parmesan and olive oil, they became something completely different: grassy, salty, creamy, and intensely spring-flavored. The day I put it on a burger was the day I stopped apologizing for putting vegetables on burgers.

Medium rare, at 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit, is the temperature that keeps the asparagus honest. The grilled spears on this burger are cooked with restraint — charred at the exterior but still snapping with some resistance inside, not limp. The patty at medium rare mirrors this philosophy: the exterior Maillard crust is fully developed, the interior is still yielding and juicy. Two ingredients treated with the same discipline — neither overcooked, both showing their best character. A well-done patty would dull the whole exercise, dragging the fresh brightness of the asparagus pesto down into heaviness. Medium rare keeps the burger in the register of spring: energetic, alive, and unmistakably seasonal.
ingredients: 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more for pan
1 lb thick asparagus stalks, tough ends removed, cut into 1-inch pieces
1/2 cup extra-virgin olive oil, plus more as needed
Fine sea salt and black pepper
2 bunches thick asparagus, tough ends snapped off
Fine sea salt and black pepper
4 oz Parmigiano-Reggiano, shaved with a vegetable peeler
2 oz prosciutto di Parma, thinly sliced (optional)
instructions: 1. Make the focaccia buns: Combine warm water, yeast, and sugar; bloom 5 minutes. Add flour, salt, and olive oil; mix until a shaggy dough forms. Knead by hand or in a mixer 8 minutes until smooth. Cover and rise 1 hour.

2. Oil a 9x13-inch baking pan generously. Press dough into pan. Drizzle olive oil over top; dimple the surface with your fingers. Scatter rosemary and flaky salt. Let proof 45 minutes. Bake at 425°F for 18–22 minutes until golden and crisp on the bottom. Cool; cut into 6 square portions and halve horizontally.

3. Make the asparagus pesto: Blanch asparagus pieces in boiling salted water 2 minutes. Transfer immediately to an ice bath; drain and pat dry. Combine in a food processor with Parmigiano, pine nuts, garlic, lemon juice, zest, and basil. Pulse while streaming in olive oil until desired consistency — keep it slightly coarse. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate.
4. Prepare the grilled asparagus: Toss asparagus spears with olive oil, lemon zest, red pepper flakes, salt, and pepper.

5. Form the patties: Season ground chuck with salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Divide into 4 portions (8 oz each). Shape into patties slightly larger than the focaccia squares, 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
6. Heat a grill or grill pan to high heat. Grill asparagus spears 2–3 minutes per side until charred and just tender. Set aside.

7. On a hot cast-iron skillet or griddle with a thin film of neutral oil, cook patties 3–4 minutes undisturbed. Flip; top each with shaved Parmigiano. Cook 2–3 minutes more. Target internal temperature 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove and tent with foil for 3 minutes.
8. Toss arugula with olive oil and lemon juice. Season.
9. Toast focaccia bun halves cut-side down in olive oil in a skillet until golden and crisp, about 90 seconds.

10. Assemble: Spread a generous layer of asparagus pesto on both cut sides of the focaccia. Place arugula on the bottom bun. Set the Parmigiano-topped patty. Drape prosciutto over if using. Arrange grilled asparagus spears across the top. Finish with flaky sea salt. Crown with the top bun.
